snapshot.title: UPSC History: Tribal & Peasant Revolts (Pre-1857)
snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC History Hook: Santhal: Sidhu/Kanhu. Munda: Birsa. Indigo: Nil Darpan. Sanyasi: Anandamath. Diku: Outsider. Rajmahal Hills: Santhal.

quick_notes.title: Sanyasi & Fakir Rebellion (1763–1800)
quick_notes.detail: Bengal. Sanyasis and Fakirs against British restrictions and high taxes. Immortalized in Bankim Chandra's "Anandamath" (Vande Mataram source).
quick_notes.explanation: The Sanyasi and Fakir Rebellion was a series of uprisings in Bengal (a region in eastern India) between 1763 and 1800, led by Hindu ascetics called Sanyasis and Muslim holy men called Fakirs. These groups rose in armed revolt against the British East India Company, which had imposed heavy taxes on the local people and banned the Sanyasis and Fakirs from traveling freely to their holy sites or collecting alms. The rebels used guerrilla tactics, raiding British treasuries and estates, and were joined by many poor peasants who were also crushed by the new tax demands. This rebellion is famously remembered today because the Bengali writer Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote the novel Anandamath (literally meaning "The Abbey of Bliss") in 1882, which features the Sanyasi fighters as heroes and contains the original version of the song Vande Mataram (meaning "I bow to the Mother"), which later became India's national song. The rebellion failed to overthrow British rule, but it showed early organized resistance against colonial authority.

quick_notes.title: Santhal Rebellion (1855–56)
quick_notes.detail: Leaders: Sidhu and Kanhu. Region : Rajmahal Hills (Daman-i-koh). Against Zamindars and "Dikus" (outsiders). It was the most massive tribal uprising before 1857.
quick_notes.explanation: The Santhal Rebellion was a large and powerful uprising of the Santhal tribal community that took place from 1855 to 1856 in the Rajmahal Hills region, an area also called Daman-i-koh. The main leaders were two brothers, Sidhu and Kanhu, who organized their people against two groups of oppressors: the Zamindars, who were local landlords, and the Dikus, a term meaning outsiders or non-tribal people who exploited them. This rebellion is considered the biggest and most widespread tribal revolt that happened in India before the major 1857 War of Independence. The Santhals rose up because they were being cheated by the Zamindars and moneylenders, and also because the British government had not kept its promises to protect their land and rights.

quick_notes.title: Munda Rebellion (Ulgulan)
quick_notes.detail: Leader: Birsa Munda (1899-1900 - Note: Post-1857 but crucial). Against "Khuntkatti" (collective land) destruction by British. Birsa was called "Dharti Aba".
quick_notes.explanation: The Munda Rebellion, also called Ulgulan, which means "great tumult" in the local language, was a major uprising led by Birsa Munda from 1899 to 1900. Birsa Munda, known as "Dharti Aba" or "Father of the Earth," fought against the British because they destroyed the traditional "Khuntkatti" system, which was a form of collective land ownership where the entire Munda community held land together. The British introduced new land laws and allowed outsiders like moneylenders and landlords to take over Munda lands, breaking this system. Birsa united the Munda tribespeople to demand the return of their land and the end of British rule, using guerrilla warfare tactics. Although the rebellion was crushed and Birsa died in British custody in 1900, it forced the British to pass the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act of 1908, which gave some legal protection to tribal land rights. This rebellion is important because it happened after the 1857 revolt and showed that tribal communities continued to resist British colonial rule.

quick_notes.title: Indigo Revolt (1859–60)
quick_notes.detail: Bengal. Peasants refused to grow Indigo under exploitative contracts. Leaders : Digambar and Bishnu Biswas. Described in "Nil Darpan" by Dinabandhu Mitra.
quick_notes.explanation: Indigo Revolt (1859-60) The Indigo Revolt was a protest by farmers in Bengal, India, against the forced cultivation of indigo, a plant used to make blue dye. British planters forced Indian peasants to sign exploitative contracts, called taccavi loans, which trapped them in debt and required them to grow indigo instead of food crops. The revolt began when peasants, led by local leaders Digambar Biswas and Bishnu Biswas, refused to plant indigo and attacked the planters' factories. The British government eventually appointed a commission to investigate, and as a result, the oppressive indigo system was largely abolished in Bengal. The play "Nil Darpan" (The Mirror of Indigo), written by Dinabandhu Mitra in 1860, vividly described the suffering of the peasants and the brutality of the planters, helping to spread awareness of the revolt.

quick_notes.title: Other Key Revolts
quick_notes.detail: Paika Rebellion (Odisha 1817 - Bakshi Jagabandhu). Ramosi Revolt (Chittur Singh). Kol Mutiny (Buddho Bhagat). Farazi Movement (Haji Shariatullah).
quick_notes.explanation: The Paika Rebellion took place in Odisha in 1817 and was led by Bakshi Jagabandhu. "Paika" means a foot soldier, and the revolt was against the British East India Company's new land revenue system and loss of power. The Ramosi Revolt was fought by the Ramosi tribal community in the Deccan region, led by Chittur Singh, against British rule and land taxes. The Kol Mutiny occurred in 1831-32 in the Chota Nagpur region, led by Buddho Bhagat, as the Kol people rose against British and moneylender exploitation. Finally, the Farazi Movement was a religious and agrarian uprising led by Haji Shariatullah, starting in 1818 in Bengal, where the "Farazis" preached a return to Islamic fundamentals and opposed taxes imposed by landlords and the British.

lesson_intro: Today we study the 'Resistance from the Grassroots'. Long before the 1857 Revolt, the peasants and tribals of India had been fighting the British and their Indian collaborators (Zamindars/Moneylenders). These revolts were localized, violent, and spontaneous reactions to the loss of land and forest rights. From the Sanyasi Rebellion to the great Santhal Hool and the Indigo Revolt—these movements proved that the British rule was never fully accepted. For UPSC, focus on the 'Leader', 'Region', and 'Cause' of each revolt.
